Unequal subproblems and Akra–Bazzi

Linear work from shrinking total mass

For T(n) = T(αn) + T(βn) + cn in an ideal real-size model with 0<α,β<1 and α + β<1, the total active size at depth j is at most n(α + β)j. Terminated nodes can only reduce that mass. Summing the internal work gives at most cn/(1 − α − β). At the fixed positive stopping threshold, base leaves also cost only O(n): their masses are bounded below by a positive constant, and splitting never increases total mass. The root's positive linear toll gives an Ω(n) lower bound. Thus this exact positive-toll recurrence has Θ(n) cost.

For a corresponding upper inequality alone, the reasoning proves O(n); a compulsory linear scan in the actual algorithm establishes tightness separately. With additive rounding error, substitution makes the margin explicit. If child sizes sum to at most γn + D with γ<1, then a linear upper guess produces Cγn + CD + cn, which is at most Cn once n is large and C exceeds c/(1 − γ). Cover the finite smaller band by a suitable base bound. This proof applies to the median-of-medians size bound without pretending the ideal fractions are exact integers.

If α + β = 1, the lost margin disappears; with linear tolls the solution is typically Θ(n log n). A longest-path upper estimate alone does not prove a matching lower estimate. If the total child ratio exceeds one, mass grows, and the leaf exponent is determined by a weighted equation rather than a fake average subproblem size.

A precise unperturbed theorem

Consider a real-size equation T(x) = ∑ aiT(bix) + g(x) above a fixed threshold, with a fixed finite number of terms, ai>0, and 0<bi<1. After a fixed rescaling of input units, use a base interval [1,x0] with x0 ≥ 1/mini bi; every child of a nonbase call then has argument at least one. Base values throughout that interval are bounded above and below by positive constants. Assume the toll is nonnegative, locally integrable, and bounded on each finite interval; extend it over the base interval as a bounded nonnegative integrable function. Assume its multiplicative-interval comparability: there are fixed A,B>0 with Ag(x) ≤ g(u) ≤ Bg(x) for every relevant u between bix and x and all sufficiently large x. This is a substantive smoothness hypothesis, not merely the statement that a derivative happens to have a polynomial bound.

There is a unique real p with ∑ aibip = 1: the left side is continuous and strictly decreasing in p, approaches infinity as p tends to negative infinity, and approaches zero at positive infinity. Under the stated assumptions,

AkraBazziintegralestimatewithitspositivebasecontribution

For actual recursive call counts, the ai are positive integers; then p ≥ 0. Fractional positive coefficients define weighted mathematical recurrences and can give a negative exponent, but do not mean that a program executes a fraction of a call. The theorem concerns an unperturbed real-size model. Its full perturbation extension has additional conditions and is not assumed for arbitrary variable child arguments.

Why the integral formula works

Define F(x) = xp(1 + ∫1x g(u)/up + 1du). Positive weights wi = aibip sum to one. Expand the child expressions and subtract them from the parent. The constant terms cancel, leaving

Definetheparentminusweightedchildrengap
Thegapisapositiveweightedsumofintegralsovershrinkingintervals

On each interval [bix,x], comparability bounds g(u) by fixed multiples of g(x), and up + 1 by fixed multiples of xp + 1. Its length is (1 − bi)x. Therefore each displayed weighted integral, after multiplying by xp, is between fixed positive multiples of g(x). Summing finitely many positive weights gives constants d,D>0 with dg(x) ≤ F(x) − ∑ aiF(bix) ≤ Dg(x).

For the upper bound, choose C ≥ 1/d and large enough for the bounded base interval. Induction gives T(x) ≤ C∑ aiF(bix) + g(x) ≤ CF(x). For the lower bound choose 0<c ≤ 1/D and small enough for all base values, giving T(x) ≥ c∑ aiF(bix) + g(x) ≥ cF(x). Both choices are made once. To make induction on real inputs precise, choose a threshold large enough that every bix lies at least one unit below x above the threshold, and induct over consecutive unit intervals. The finite transition interval is absorbed into the base constants. This proves the unperturbed formula without requiring equal-depth leaves.

For g(x) = Θ(xq(log x)k), the integral is comparable to integrating uq − p − 1(log u)k, away from a fixed initial cutoff. When q<p it converges for any fixed real k; when q>p it grows as xq − p(log x)k; when q = p, substitute v = log u and use the three log-power thresholds. The resulting classification agrees with the equal-size master analysis and extends it to unequal constant ratios.

Do not apply this integral theorem to exponential tolls merely because the recurrence has shrinking children. For a regular exponential toll such as 2n, direct comparison or unrolling can show root dominance, but the polynomial-interval comparability required here fails.

Changes of variables and resource models

Transform the argument, not the answer

For T(n) = 2T(√n) + log2 n on n = 22h, first set m = log2 n and S(m) = T(2m). The equation becomes S(m) = 2S(m/2) + m, so S(m) = Θ(m log m). Returning to the original variable gives T(n) = Θ(log n log log n). Reporting Θ(n log n) would forget the transformation and solve the wrong problem.

For T(n) = T(√n) + 1 with a constant threshold greater than one, log size halves on each call. There are Θ(log log n) calls. But T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 has Θ(log n) calls. A square root, a constant-factor reduction, and a constant decrement are three different progress rates; visually similar short formulas do not imply similar depths.

For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/log2 n, the substitution n = 2h and U(h) = T(2h)/2h yields U(h) = U(h − 1) + 1/h, with a base at h = 1. Thus U(h) is harmonic and the original answer is Θ(n log log n). Normalizing by the leaf exponent often reveals the sum responsible for a difficult boundary case.

Work, span, storage, and repeated states

Two independent half-size calls with a linear combine step have sequential work W(n) = 2W(n/2) + Θ(n). If the calls run in parallel but combining is sequential, span satisfies S(n) = S(n/2) + Θ(n), which is linear. A parallel combine step with logarithmic span instead gives S(n) = S(n/2) + Θ(log n), producing Θ((log n)2). Processor scheduling and actual parallel primitives must support the claimed span model.

Stack space follows the maximum simultaneously live chain and per-frame storage. With constant-size frames and sequential half-size recursion, stack use is Θ(log n), even when total work is Θ(n log n). If each live frame retains an array proportional to its local size, the maximum sum along a halving path is linear. If temporary memory is released before the child calls, that storage recurrence changes. Space is a liveness question, not a copy of the time equation.

Naive Fibonacci recursion has repeated states and exponentially many calls. Memoizing it changes the execution graph: only linearly many distinct arguments are computed, and each performs constant work in a unit-cost arithmetic model. The recursion depth can still be linear. Fibonacci outputs have growing bit lengths, so treating arithmetic as unit cost and treating bit complexity are different analyses. A memoized implementation cannot be analyzed as if both subtrees were independently recomputed.

Expected cost must average actual conditional subproblem costs. In general E[T(X)] ≠ T(E[X]). For example, a child size equally likely to be zero or two has expected size one, but for squared cost its expected cost is two instead of one. Use conditioning and linearity of expectation to derive an expected recurrence; do not feed the average size into a nonlinear running-time function. Full probabilistic algorithm analysis is taught later.

Teaching through formulas and conceptual decisions

Account for a whole level before summing the tree

For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n) on n=bh, depth i has ai nodes, each of size n/bi. Its toll is aif(n/bi). The leaf contribution is ahT(1)=nlogbaT(1). Every proposed total must include both internal work and leaves. If f is stated only as an upper bound, the equation may not determine a tight internal-work rate, although a leaf lower bound can remain decisive.

For the balanced critical recurrence with a=b, toll n(logn)q and a positive constant base cutoff, reindex levels by distance from the leaves. Total internal work has order n∑j=1hjq. This yields nlogq+1n when q>-1, nloglogn when q=-1, and n when q<-1, after adding the linear leaves. The logarithmic denominator must be defined only above the stated cutoff; evaluating a toll n/logn at 1 is invalid.

Change variables when arguments are not linear fractions

For T(n)=T(n)+1, let n=22k and set U(k)=T(22k). Then U(k)=U(k-1)+1, so T(n) is order loglogn. For T(n)=2T(n)+log2n, instead set m=log2n and U(m)=T(2m); the equation becomes U(m)=2U(m/2)+m. Its solution is Θ(mlogm), giving Θ(lognloglogn). Translate back to the original variable at the end.

Unequal split exponents and resources

For T(n)=T(n/3)+T(2n/3)+n with admissible rounding and positive base cost, the Akra–Bazzi exponent p satisfies (1/3)p+(2/3)p=1, giving p=1. The integral correction from the linear toll is logarithmic, so the result is nlogn. Work sums child costs; parallel span can instead take their maximum. Storage of a depth-first implementation counts simultaneously live data, not every node ever created.

Deeper recurrence constructions and proof repairs

This section extends the complete lesson; it does not replace the full prerequisite instruction or the forty derivation tutorials. Its models are explicit mathematical recurrences. An algorithmic upper inequality, an equality and a lower bound are identified separately.

Construction 1. Derive the complete level sum before classifying it

Let the input be exactly N=bh, where b>1 is fixed, and let the mathematical recurrence be T(N)=aT(N/b)+f(N) with a>0 and seed T(1)=c. For an actual call tree, a must be a positive integer; the algebraic recurrence also permits positive noninteger weights. Repeated substitution proves the exact identity

T(bh)=ahc+∑j=0h−1ajf(bh−j).

The first term is the complete base contribution. The index j is depth from the root; h−j is the remaining logarithmic size. The identity follows by induction on h: multiplying the corresponding child identity by a shifts every depth by one, and the root adds the missing j=0 toll. Thus a fully counted tree, with a stopping rule and a justified sum, is already a proof.

For f(N)=Nd, put q=a/bd. The internal sum is Nd∑j=0h−1qj. If q<1, a finite geometric sum gives root domination; if q=1, every internal level contributes Nd and the count of levels supplies a factor logN; if q>1, later levels dominate. In the last case, the internal sum and the positive base contribution both have order Nlogba. These calculations establish lower bounds as well as upper bounds when the toll and bases are positive as stated. If the source specifies only f∈O(Nd), the same calculation supplies an upper envelope, not a matching positive toll automatically.

There is no rule that multiplies an arbitrary root toll by depth. One half-size child with linear toll has geometrically decreasing level work and linear total. Two half-size children have constant linear aggregate work and Θ(NlogN) total. Four have increasing aggregate work and quadratic total. The difference is multiplicity, even when the shrink map and root toll are identical.

Construction 2. Every real logarithmic power at the critical exponent

Put p=logba. Assume f(N)=Np(logbN)k for N>b, with a separately defined positive bounded base region containing N≤b. This avoids evaluating a negative power of zero at N=1. On exact powers, normalization by Np gives a weighted harmonic sum with the depth direction reversed:

T(bh)bph=C+∑r=2hrk.

The constant C>0 incorporates the base threshold. For k>−1, integral comparison bounds the sum above and below by positive multiples of hk+1. For k=−1, it is a harmonic sum of order logh. For k<−1, it converges to a finite positive limit and is bounded below by its positive seed. Therefore

  • For k>−1, the answer is T(N)∈Θ(Np(logN)k+1).
  • For k=−1, the answer is T(N)∈Θ(NploglogN).
  • For k<−1, the answer is T(N)∈Θ(Np).

The threshold is negative one, not zero. A reciprocal logarithm gives a double logarithm, while a reciprocal squared logarithm gives no unbounded extra factor. These are independently derived extensions of the level identity; a university theorem stated only for nonnegative integer logarithmic powers must not be cited as if its statement covered every real k.

For k=−1, the explicit bounds log(h+1)−log2≤∑r=2h1/r≤1+logh show where the double logarithm comes from. For k=−2, the upper bound ∑r=2∞r−2≤∫1∞x−2dx=1 gives a finite normalized envelope. Keeping the positive normalized base supplies the matching lower bound in both cases.

Construction 3. Integer stopping rules and square-root rounding

A nonlinear shrink must first be transformed. For T(N)=aT(⌊N⌋)+log2N, use m=log2N. For N≥4, the transformed child lies in [m/2−1,m/2]. After j steps, its logarithmic size lies in [m/2j−2,m/2j], obtained by summing the geometrically damped one-unit errors. For two children, the total level toll is therefore at most m and at least m−2j+1 while the full level stays above the fixed base. The first Θ(logm) levels each cost a positive multiple of m, and the entire tree has O(m) leaves. This is a direct rounding proof of Θ(mlogm).

For the exact grid N=22h with a base at two, the square root decrements h and the logarithmic toll is 2h. Thus Uh=2Uh−1+2h with U0=1, giving (h+1)2h exactly. Restoring the original variable is a second mandatory step: h=log2log2N and 2h=log2N. Neither h nor m is the original input.

By contrast, N−⌈N⌉ is a slowly shrinking chain. Its square-root potential decreases by a number between one-half and two on each step. Its depth is Θ(N), not Θ(loglogN). Similar-looking square-root notation can denote fundamentally different maps. The fixed base must also stop at any fixed point of the map: square-root recursion at one never progresses.

Construction 4. Unequal branches and the critical exponent

For an unperturbed recurrence T(x)=∑i=1raiT(bix)+g(x), assume fixed ai>0, 0<bi<1, a fixed terminal interval with bounded positive costs, and the regularity hypotheses stated in the source theorem. The critical exponent p is the unique real solution of ∑iaibip=1. Uniqueness follows because the left side is continuous and strictly decreasing in p, ranging from infinity to zero. The retained theorem states

T(x)∈Θ(xp(1+∫1xg(u)up+1du)).

The integral's lower endpoint can be any fixed positive threshold appropriate to the toll; changing it adds a constant to the normalized expression. It cannot be placed at a logarithmic singularity without qualification. For two mass-conserving children, b1+b2=1, a1=a2=1 gives p=1. A linear toll then integrates to logx. A quadratic toll integrates to order x, giving quadratic total. For 2T(x/2)+3T(x/3), the exponent solves 2(1/2)p+3(1/3)p=1; it is neither a two-child nor a three-child equal-split exponent.

The theorem is not a license to insert arbitrary rounding maps, variable ratios, or oscillating tolls outside its hypotheses. Whenever a concrete tree or induction proof is short, it gives a clearer independently checked result. For 2T(x/2)+3T(x/3)+x2, the squared-size coefficient is 2/4+3/9=5/6, so Cx2 is an upper envelope when C≥6 and the base is covered. The root supplies the lower bound. No numerical approximation of the branching exponent is needed for this example.

Construction 5. Exact balanced merging away from powers of two

Define a mathematical size-toll recurrence by A(1)=0 and A(n)=A(⌊n/2⌋)+A(⌈n/2⌉)+n for integers n≥2. Put L=⌊log2n⌋. All depths below L are complete and contribute total size n. At depth L, nodes have sizes one or two; the number of size-two nodes is n−2L, each contributing two. Thus

A(n)=nL+2(n−2L).

Ordinary worst-case merge comparisons have local toll n−1, not n. A full binary partition tree with n singleton leaves has exactly n−1 internal nodes. Consequently subtracting one per internal node gives

C(n)=A(n)−(n−1)=nL+n−2L+1+1.

Equivalently, with H=⌈log2n⌉, this is nH−2H+1; the two expressions agree at powers of two and between them. For n=13, A(13)=49 and C(13)=37. These exact recurrences model different counted operations even though both have Θ(nlogn) order. Achieving the merge comparison maximum recursively requires interleaving child outputs; the comparison recurrence here explicitly counts that worst-case arrangement rather than claiming every input has its maximum. Constant leaf work would add its own n -fold contribution.

Construction 6. Nonconstant multipliers and normalization

For Tn=anTn−1+bn with every an≠0, define P0=1 and Pn=∏j=1naj. Dividing the equation by Pn gives

TnPn=Tn−1Pn−1+bnPn,Tn=Pn(T0+∑j=1nbjPj).

This is an exact identity proved by telescoping; convergence is irrelevant for a finite sum. If a multiplier is zero, division by the product fails. At that index the recurrence resets to the current toll; restart the product after it rather than divide by zero. For signed multipliers, exact cancellation can occur, so positive-tree lower-bound arguments are inapplicable without further conditions.

The sequence Tn=nTn−1+n! with T0=1 has Pn=n!, so Tn/n!=1+n and Tn=(n+1)n!. An asymptotic answer of order n! would be too small by the unbounded factor n+1. The authentic product question has bn=0 and an=2n, yielding Pn=2n(n+1)/2. Taking logarithms is convenient only when the values are positive; it does not repair a zero or negative-value domain.

Construction 7. Expected cost requires conditioning

If a random child size is J, the expected recurrence contains 𝔼[T(J)], not generally T(𝔼[J]). The latter replacement would need extra properties, and it is false in general: for equally likely sizes one and three and T(j)=j2, the first expression is five while the second is four.

For an illustrative uniform-pivot process that always follows the larger child, J=max(R,n−1−R) for uniform rank R in 0,…,n−1. Conditional on the current input, explicitly average every rank. For even n=2m, each size m,…,2m−1 occurs twice, so 𝔼[J]=(3m−1)/2=3n/4−1/2. For odd n=2m+1, size m occurs once and each size m+1,…,2m twice; the mean is (3m2+2m)/(2m+1), below 3n/4. The pointwise induction hypothesis T(j)≤Cj therefore gives 𝔼[T(J)]≤C𝔼[J]≤3Cn/4. With toll at most cn, choosing C≥4c closes the upper induction after covering bases. A compulsory linear root scan gives the lower bound and hence expected Θ(n) work for this stated process.

This argument uses a linear envelope after conditioning. It does not assume the unknown expected-cost function commutes with expectation. Actual QuickSelect may follow a smaller child for some target ranks, which only reduces this upper envelope. A worst-case pivot sequence remains a different model and can be quadratic. Probabilistic claims require specifying both the distribution and the conditioning state.

Construction 8. Reconcile source errors before borrowing formulas

The four principal course scopes and Cornell supplement were actually read. Their disagreements are resolved by derivation. MIT's supplemental Akra–Bazzi example has critical exponent two and toll Θ(x2/logx) beyond a fixed threshold. Its normalized integral is ∫du/(ulogu)=loglogu, so the answer multiplies by loglogx. The source's printed division by that factor is an error. The same proof's final lower-constant line needs the lower toll constant, not the upper one. The chapter uses independently verified statements rather than copying these lines.

A polynomial bound on the derivative alone does not establish uniform multiplicative comparability of a nonnegative toll: g(x)=sin2x has bounded derivative but infinitely many zeros. Cornell's unequal-tree discussion prints a different equation than its intended one-third/two-thirds tree; the child sizes in the diagram and recurrence must agree. Its substitution comparison must recur on the envelope itself, rather than mix unknown original children into its definition.

Stanford's notes identify Winter 2026 in the actual retrieved header despite the URL's 2025 path. Its polynomial-toll theorem is an upper-bound formulation. MIT's recurrence exercises also use upper inequalities in places. A claimed tight class is supported here by a separate lower proof or exact positive recurrence. Princeton's size-toll merge formula is kept distinct from comparisons with toll size minus one. These repairs are recorded with exact reading scopes; screened universities are not represented as courses whose full notes were read.

Ten solved transfer challenges

These are newly worded mathematical problems informed by the reviewed university material. They are not represented as additional authentic Iranian questions or as verbatim university assessment questions. Each recurrence has a declared domain and base. The questions combine symbolic classification with a complete proof or exact calculation.

Challenge 1. Five quarter-size children and a linear toll

The input, base region, cost model and exact checkpoint are declared. Complete level aggregates, full state lists and illustrative tree fragments are distinguished explicitly.

Problem. On N=4h, define T(1)=1 and T(N)=5T(N/4)+2N. Find an exact expression, its tight order, the number of depth-four descendants and the first input depth with descendant size N/1024.

Solution. At depth j there are 5j nodes of size N/4j, so the combined toll is 2N(5/4)j. The leaves cost 5h. Summing the finite geometric progression gives

T(4h)=5h+2·4h(5/4)h−11/4=9·5h−8·4h.

The seed at h=0 is one. At h=1, the original recurrence gives 5+8=13, matching 45−32. The critical exponent is log45>1, so the tight order is Θ(Nlog45). Depth four contains 54=625 descendants, provided the root is large enough to reach that depth. Dividing size by 1024 requires five quartering steps, since 45=1024; branch multiplicity five does not determine size reduction. At h=5, the exact total is 19933. The model keeps the terminal contribution separate from the increasing internal level costs. This is an exact variant of the Stanford concept check, with a specified seed added by the author.

Challenge 2. A critical fourth-root exponent

The input, base region, cost model and exact checkpoint are declared. Complete level aggregates, full state lists and illustrative tree fragments are distinguished explicitly.

Problem. For N=81h, define T(1)=1 and T(N)=3T(N/81)+10N1/4. Obtain the exact total and classify it.

Solution. Because 811/4=3, the branching exponent is p=log813=1/4. At depth j, combined toll is 3j10(N/81j)1/4=10N1/4. There are exactly h internal depths, and the 3h=N1/4 unit leaves contribute another N1/4. Hence

T(81h)=(10h+1)3h.

For depth four, the value is 41·81=3321. Normalization also proves it: Uh=T(81h)/3h satisfies Uh=Uh−1+10 with U0=1. Restoring h=log81N gives Θ(N1/4logN). Keeping N1/4 without the depth factor would lose all but a constant number of equal-cost levels. Conversely, multiplying by the original input rather than h would confuse the two variables. The model explicitly labels input, multiplicity, local toll, aggregate toll and leaf work. This is independently derived from the reviewed critical-case example.

Challenge 3. Two logarithmic thresholds on the same tree

The input, base region, cost model and exact checkpoint are declared. Complete level aggregates, full state lists and illustrative tree fragments are distinguished explicitly.

Problem. For N=2h, stop at N≤2 with cost one. For larger inputs define Tk(N)=2Tk(N/2)+N/(log2N)k. Compare k=1 and k=2, with exact normalized finite sums.

Solution. Write Vh=Tk(2h)/2h. The base is V1=1/2. Dividing each step gives Vh=Vh−1+1/hk, hence

Tk(2h)=2h(12+∑r=2h1rk).

For k=1, harmonic integral bounds give a normalized value of order logh, so T1(N)∈Θ(NloglogN). For k=2, the normalized sum stays between 1/2 and 3/2, so T2(N)∈Θ(N). The unit base supplies the strictly positive lower constant even when the toll sum converges. At h=4, the exact totals are T1(16)=76/3 and T2(16)=133/9; these are mathematical costs with rational tolls, not literal integer operation counts.

The threshold at N=2 prevents division by zero at N=1. A nonnegative-log-power-only Master theorem does not cover these tolls. The finite normalized sum directly proves them and explains why a reciprocal logarithm and its square have different outcomes. The animation plots the actual finite terms and partial sums for each scenario rather than using the same generic tree for both.

Challenge 4. A regularity counterexample with positive polynomial tolls

The input, base region, cost model and exact checkpoint are declared. Complete level aggregates, full state lists and illustrative tree fragments are distinguished explicitly.

Problem. On N=2h, let T(1)=1 and T(N)=2T(N/2)+f(N), where f(N)=N3 at even h and f(N)=N2 at odd h. Determine the tight order and explain why a root-dominated Master conclusion fails.

Solution. The toll is always at most N3. Its complete-tree upper sum is bounded by N3∑j≥04−j plus N unit leaf work, so T(N)=O(N3). At even h, the root supplies N3. At odd h≥3, its two children have even logarithmic depth and each contributes root toll (N/2)3, totaling N3/4. Therefore every sufficiently large grid input has a cubic lower bound and T(N)∈Θ(N3).

Although f(N)≥N2 is polynomially above the critical leaf exponent one, regularity fails at odd depths:

2f(N/2)f(N)=N4.

No constant less than one bounds that ratio. At the same odd inputs, T(N)/f(N)≥N/4→∞, refuting T∈Θ(f) for this toll. The exact sequence at depths zero through five is 1,6,76,216,4528,10080. Every value includes both the appropriate current toll and twice the previous value. Polynomial dominance alone is insufficient for that version of the root case; the regularity condition serves a mathematical purpose.

Challenge 5. Mixed child sizes with a quadratic toll

The input, base region, cost model and exact checkpoint are declared. Complete level aggregates, full state lists and illustrative tree fragments are distinguished explicitly.

Problem. Consider the unperturbed real-size recurrence T(x)=2T(x/2)+3T(x/3)+x2 above a fixed base threshold. Base costs are bounded and positive. Find its tight order using a complete induction envelope.

Solution. The root toll gives T(x)≥x2 at every nonbase input. For the upper bound, suppose smaller nonbase and base arguments satisfy T(y)≤Cy2. A terminal interval must be chosen bounded away from zero for this envelope, or use an equivalent positive constant addition to the envelope at smaller inputs. Above a suitable fixed threshold the direct calculation is

T(x)≤C(2x24+3x29)+x2=(5C6+1)x2.

Taking C≥6 makes this at most Cx2, and increasing C covers every terminal argument reachable from a parent just above the threshold. A rigorous real-size induction can proceed on intervals whose width is fixed and whose children lie in earlier intervals; the threshold is enlarged if necessary. Thus T(x)=O(x2) and the root lower bound gives Θ(x2).

The branching equation is 2(1/2)p+3(1/3)p=1. Its left side is 5/6 at p=2, so its unique solution lies below two; this corroborates the quadratic toll dominance. Replacing the expression by five equal children would be a different recurrence. The compact diagram displays two half-size and three third-size branches, together with their individual quadratic weights. The constant six follows from the slack 1−5/6, not from the number of branches alone.

Challenge 6. Exact merge work at thirteen elements

The input, base region, cost model and exact checkpoint are declared. Complete level aggregates, full state lists and illustrative tree fragments are distinguished explicitly.

Problem. Balanced recursive merging stops at singleton arrays. Compute the size-toll total and the worst-case comparison total for thirteen elements; prove the general formulas.

Solution. With L=⌊log2n⌋, the first L complete depths each have total active size n. At depth L, the balanced nodes have size one or two. There are n−2L size-two nodes and their size toll adds 2(n−2L). Thus A(n)=nL+2n−2L+1. The full binary tree has n singleton leaves and n−1 internal nodes. Ordinary worst-case merging uses size minus one comparisons, so subtracting one at every internal node gives C(n)=nL+n−2L+1+1.

For thirteen, L=3, and

A(13)=39+26−16=49,C(13)=49−12=37.

Direct recurrence checking gives C(6)=11, C(7)=14 and C(13)=11+14+12=37. For the size toll, A(6)=16, A(7)=20 and A(13)=16+20+13=49. The two totals share the same recursive partition but count different local operations. The animation reveals the actual rounded split tree and an exact depth ledger, including the incomplete final internal depth; it never labels thirteen as a power of two.

This is an independently specified recurrence calculation. An implementation's actual comparisons depend on its input order. The word worst case here includes the standard interleavings that make each merge perform the full size-minus-one count. A unit leaf cost would add thirteen to either zero-leaf model and must be stated separately.

Challenge 7. A factorial multiplier with a nonzero toll

The input, base region, cost model and exact checkpoint are declared. Complete level aggregates, full state lists and illustrative tree fragments are distinguished explicitly.

Problem. Let T0=1 and Tn=nTn−1+n! for n≥1. Derive an exact solution and decide whether Θ(n!) is a valid tight answer.

Solution. Divide by n! and put Vn=Tn/n!. The coefficient cancels exactly: nTn−1/n!=Tn−1/(n−1)!. Hence Vn=Vn−1+1, with V0=1. It follows that

Tn=(n+1)n!.

For n=5, T5=6·120=720. Iteration gives 1,2,6,24,120,720, matching the closed form at every shown index. Induction verifies n[n(n−1)!]+n!=(n+1)n!; the base is also correct. The order is Θ(nn!) for positive large n, not Θ(n!), because the quotient by n! is n+1→∞.

The product normalizer is nonzero at every index, including 0!=1, so division is justified. If a different problem introduced a zero multiplier, the normalizer would fail and the recurrence would need to restart at that index. Omitting the toll would yield just n!, demonstrating precisely where the extra factor arises. This example extends the first-order variable-coefficient normalization in the Princeton scope and keeps the exact finite sum rather than replacing it by a vague dominant multiplier.

Challenge 8. Expected size and expected cost

The input, base region, cost model and exact checkpoint are declared. Complete level aggregates, full state lists and illustrative tree fragments are distinguished explicitly.

Problem. A process on four elements chooses a pivot rank uniformly in 0,1,2,3 and follows its larger partition. Let that partition size be J. First compare 𝔼[J2] with (𝔼[J])2. Then prove a linear expected upper bound for the corresponding recurrence with linear toll at general size.

Solution. The four equally likely sizes are 3,2,2,3. Therefore

𝔼[J]=52,𝔼[J2]=132,(𝔼[J])2=254.

The two quadratic quantities differ by one-quarter. A recurrence involving expected child cost therefore cannot replace that cost by the cost of the average child without a separate justification.

For general n, uniform ranks give 𝔼[J]≤3n/4 by explicitly summing the symmetric rank distribution. Assume a pointwise induction envelope for every smaller size: T(j)≤Cj. Taking its conditional expectation preserves the inequality and gives 𝔼[T(J)]≤C𝔼[J]≤3Cn/4. If the local toll is at most cn, choosing C≥4c closes the bound, with bases included by increasing C. A compulsory linear scan supplies Ω(n) expected work, so the tight class is Θ(n) for this stated process.

The expectation is conditional on the current size and a newly uniform pivot. A deterministic adversarial pivot distribution does not satisfy the same mean-shrink bound. The diagram shows all four outcomes with their probabilities, means and second moments rather than animating a fictitious child of fractional size 2.5.

Challenge 9. Exact exponential comparison

The input, base region, cost model and exact checkpoint are declared. Complete level aggregates, full state lists and illustrative tree fragments are distinguished explicitly.

Problem. For T0=1 and Tn=2nTn−1, compare its exact answer with 2n2 and 2n2/2. Which, if either, is in the same tight class?

Solution. Expanding the changing multipliers gives Tn=2n(n+1)/2. Relative to 2n2, the ratio is 2(−n2+n)/2→0, so that larger exponential is not a matching tight answer. Relative to 2n2/2, the ratio is 2n/2→∞, so even deleting only the linear part of the exponent changes the tight class. Neither is in Θ(Tn).

The exact expression (2)n2+n is in that class by equality. A constant additive error in the exponent would produce a bounded positive multiplicative factor; a linear or quadratic unbounded exponent error generally would not. For example, multiplying Tn by two changes the exponent by one and preserves its tight class. Replacing the exponent by its leading polynomial term does not.

At n=4, the actual value is 1024, while the two proposed values are 65536 and 256. The logarithmic display records these exponents 10,16,8 exactly and continues through several indices so the changing differences are visible. Finite data is illustrative; the two ratio limits are the proof. This example tests exponential sensitivity rather than applying a polynomial simplification rule in the wrong domain.

Challenge 10. A DAG reduction with a changed local toll

The input, base region, cost model and exact checkpoint are declared. Complete level aggregates, full state lists and illustrative tree fragments are distinguished explicitly.

Problem. A program requests the same half-size state twice but reuses the first result. Its local work is log2N, its unit base is at one, and N=2h. Find the exact reused cost and compare it with the unreused version.

Solution. The reused program executes one recursive child, so Uh=Uh−1+h with U0=1. It follows that

Uh=1+h(h+1)2,

which is Θ((logN)2) in the original size. At N=32, h=5 and the cost is 16. In contrast, two executed children give Vh=2Vh−1+h with V0=1. The zero-seed weighted-index solution plus the homogeneous seed yields Vh=3·2h−h−2. At h=5 this equals 89 and has order Θ(N).

Both programs have logarithmic depth and the same local toll, but their total executed work differs because one follows a chain and the other expands a binary tree. The recursion arguments refer to the identical state, not simply two different states of equal size. A bounded lookup per reuse adds a bounded cost per level and preserves the reused quadratic-logarithm order, although its exact polynomial constant changes. The model labels the reused edge as a reference, not an extra executed child, and shows the two exact ledgers side by side through every transformed index.

Each exact formula satisfies its own seed and step equation. Confusing the two child counts or dropping the unit leaf seed would change the finite values, even where the broad growth class stayed the same.

Detailed derivation tutorials

The following complete proofs and implementations support the new examination problems. They develop the reasoning needed to derive formulas; the separately labeled examination bank below tests calculation, concepts and distractor decisions.

Tutorial 1. A recurrence does not yet specify a function

Original · Domains and base cases. An author writes T(n) = T(⌈2n/3⌉) + 1 for every integer n>1, with T(1) = 1. Diagnose the model and repair it.

Solution. At two the child size is ⌈4/3⌉ = 2, so the definition demands T(2) = T(2) + 1, impossible for a finite value. The recurrence has a familiar constant reduction only at sufficiently large inputs. Set a base cost at two as well, and apply the recursive rule only for n ≥ 3. For those inputs the ceiling is at most n − 1, so strong induction gives a unique finite sequence. A constant-size base range does not change its logarithmic asymptotic depth, but the original self-reference was mathematically invalid. Check small inputs before applying any solution theorem.

Tutorial 2. One branch, two calls, or a cached result

Original · Model derivation. Compare a half-size recursion called twice sequentially, a conditional selecting one half-size call, and one computed half-size result reused twice. Assume a unit local toll and constant positive bases.

Solution. The first model is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1, yielding linear work from its binary tree. The conditional executes one child, so its model is T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 and its work is logarithmic. Reusing an already computed result also executes one recursive call, with only constant local reuse work, so it follows the second model. A source expression containing the child function twice may or may not execute it twice, depending on whether the result is stored. Derive the execution structure before selecting a branching coefficient. The number of distinct subproblem sizes does not equal the number of uncached calls.

Tutorial 3. Why an upper toll does not give a tight bound

Course-derived · Stanford's explicit upper-bound formulation; original counterexample. Does T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) force T(n) = Θ(n log n)?

Solution. No. Set the actual toll to one and the base at one to one. This is a permitted O(n) toll, but the exact recurrence has solution 2n − 1 on powers of two: its binary tree has n leaves and n − 1 internal nodes. The standard linear envelope gives an O(n log n) upper bound, but no matching lower bound follows from that information. If the actual toll is bounded below by a positive multiple of n at each sufficiently large call and bases are positive, level sums give the tight result. The missing lower assumption changes the logical strength of the conclusion.

Tutorial 4. Binary search with a costly representation

Course-derived · MIT Recitation 3 binary-search exercise, extended cost model. Compare index-based binary search with an implementation that copies the chosen half of the input array before each recursive call.

Solution. Index boundaries take constant local work, giving T(n) = T(⌊n/2⌋) + Θ(1) and Θ(log n) time. Copying a half costs Θ(n) at a size-n node, so the second model is U(n) = U(⌊n/2⌋) + Θ(n). Its copied sizes form a geometric sequence n,n/2,n/4,…, summing to linear time. The second implementation still makes logarithmically many comparisons, but its total time is linear in this representation. Naming the algorithm is insufficient to determine all resource costs; identify the operation being counted and whether the data are copied or viewed.

Tutorial 5. An exact additive chain

Course-derived · MIT additive recurrence exercise, exact toll and base. Solve T(0) = 4 and T(n) = T(n − 1) + 3n + 2.

Solution. Expand through the base: T(n) = 4 + ∑j = 1n(3j + 2) = 4 + 3n(n + 1)/2 + 2n. Thus the exact answer is (3n2 + 7n + 8)/2. Its value at zero is four. Subtracting its value at n − 1 gives exactly 3n + 2, proving it satisfies every recurrence step; uniqueness supplies completeness. The quadratic leading term gives Θ(n2), while omitting the initial four would produce a different exact sequence. An asymptotic answer and an exact answer have different obligations.

Tutorial 6. Additive power thresholds

Original · Integral bounds. For T(n) = T(n − 1) + nr, T(0) = 1, classify the growth for fixed real r.

Solution. The exact expression is 1 + ∑j = 1njr. If r> − 1, upper and lower rectangle comparisons with xr give order nr + 1; for nonnegative r, the last-half lower bound is an alternative proof. At r =  − 1, the sum is harmonic and grows logarithmically. If r< − 1, its infinite positive sum converges, while the initial one keeps a positive lower bound, giving constant order. The often-used exponent-plus-one rule has a domain restriction. Fractional tolls here define a mathematical cost model; they need not be literal integer operation counts.

Tutorial 7. Exponential size from a linear-depth tree

Course-derived · MIT's double-call decrement exercise; exact base. Solve T(0) = 1 and T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1.

Solution. Divide the normalized expression by 2n, or expand all calls. The result is T(n) = 2n + ∑j = 1n2n − j = 2n + 1 − 1. At depth j there are 2j nodes, and the depth is n. The longest path is linear, but the node population is exponential. Substitution verifies 2(2n − 1) + 1 = 2n + 1 − 1. A linear call-stack bound is therefore compatible with exponential total work. The exact leading coefficient also depends on the specified base value.

Tutorial 8. A summation factor with variable coefficients

Course-derived · Princeton Exercise 2.13, independently derived. Solve A0 = 1 and An = (n/(n + 1))An − 1 + 1.

Solution. The product of multipliers through n telescopes to 1/(n + 1). Set Bn = (n + 1)An. Multiplying the recurrence by n + 1 gives Bn = Bn − 1 + n + 1, with B0 = 1. Hence Bn = 1 + n(n + 3)/2 = (n + 1)(n + 2)/2, so An = (n + 2)/2. The initial value checks, and direct substitution gives the same formula at every step. Using a constant-coefficient characteristic equation would be inappropriate because the multiplier depends on n; normalization restores a simple additive recurrence.

Tutorial 9. A zero multiplier resets a chain

Original · Summation-factor boundary. Suppose A0 = 10, A1 = 2A0 + 3, A2 = 0A1 + 5, and An = 2An − 1 + 1 for n ≥ 3. Find an exact expression from index two onward.

Solution. The first value is twenty-three, but the zero multiplier makes A2 = 5, independent of everything before it. Restart at index two. Expansion of the later recurrence gives An = 2n − 2·5 + (2n − 2 − 1) = 6·2n − 2 − 1. At two this is five, and its subsequent difference equation checks directly. Dividing by the product of multipliers from zero would divide by zero, so the summation-factor formula cannot cross that step. A reset is part of the recurrence's exact structure, not a negligible asymptotic adjustment.

Tutorial 10. Distinct characteristic roots and cancellation

Original · Linear recurrence. Solve An = 3An − 1 − 2An − 2 with A0 = 4, A1 = 6. Then change the initial pair to (4,4).

Solution. The characteristic polynomial factors as (λ − 1)(λ − 2). Thus An = u + v2n. The initial equations are u + v = 4 and u + 2v = 6, giving u = v = 2 and An = 2 + 2n + 1. For the alternative pair, the equations give v = 0, so the sequence is the constant four. The largest root is two in both recurrences, but its coefficient vanishes in the second solution. Initial values can remove a dominant mode. Check both base equations and the recurrence instead of assigning exponential growth from the characteristic polynomial alone.

Tutorial 11. A repeated root needs another factor

Original · Repeated-root equation. Solve An = 4An − 1 − 4An − 2, with A0 = 1 and A1 = 4.

Solution. The characteristic polynomial is (λ − 2)2. The independent solutions are 2n and n2n, so use (u + vn)2n. The bases yield u = 1 and 2(1 + v) = 4, giving v = 1. The answer is (n + 1)2n. Substituting verifies that 4n2n − 1 − 4(n − 1)2n − 2 = (n + 1)2n. The second solution's linear factor is necessary to accommodate arbitrary two base values. Treating a repeated root as two identical exponentials would collapse the two-dimensional solution family to one dimension.

Tutorial 12. Resonance in a forced equation

Original · Nonhomogeneous recurrence. Solve An = 2An − 1 + 2n, A0 = 3.

Solution. Let Bn = An/2n. The recurrence becomes Bn = Bn − 1 + 1, with B0 = 3. Therefore Bn = n + 3 and An = (n + 3)2n. A particular solution of the form c2n cannot work: subtracting twice its predecessor gives zero, while the forcing is nonzero. Multiplication by n provides the needed independent shape. This is the elementary resonance rule in a form whose normalization and exact initial coefficient are completely visible.

Tutorial 13. Count a complete recursion level

Course-derived · Stanford solved concept-check tree, independently explained. For T(n) = 5T(n/4) + 2n, determine node count at depth four, size at depth five, and internal cost at depth j.

Solution. Each node creates five children, so depth four contains 54 = 625 nodes. Each step divides size by four, so every depth-five node has size n/45 = n/1024. At depth j, multiply node count by each node's toll: 5j·2(n/4j) = 2n(5/4)j. The total increases geometrically down the internal levels. Positive leaves contribute order nlog4 5, consistent with the leaf-dominated master result. The reciprocal ratio (4/5)j would incorrectly combine branching and shrinking in reverse. These statements concern existing internal levels; a level below the stopping depth does not exist.

Tutorial 14. Exact balanced level costs

Original · Tree identity. Solve T(1) = 2 and T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n on powers of two.

Solution. Let h = log2 n. Each of the h internal levels contributes exactly n; there are n leaves at cost two each. Thus T(n) = n log2 n + 2n. At one the log term is zero and the value is two. Substitution gives 2[(n/2)(log2 n − 1) + n] + n = n log2 n + 2n. This proves both the exact identity and its order Θ(n log n). Counting the leaves as another linear toll level would give the wrong coefficient because their base cost is two, not the internal toll convention.

Tutorial 15. The root dominates a geometric tree

Course-derived · Cornell's quadratic binary-tree example; exact base. Solve T(1) = 1 and T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n2 for powers of two.

Solution. Internal levels cost n2, n2/2,…,n2/2h − 1. Their sum is 2n2(1 − 1/n) = 2n2 − 2n. The leaves contribute n, giving T(n) = 2n2 − n. The exact value satisfies both the base and recurrence. The ratio one half makes the total a constant multiple of the root contribution, so the depth is not another multiplicative log factor. Adding a logarithm merely because recursion has logarithmic depth would overestimate the tight answer.

Tutorial 16. Leaves dominate despite cheap internal calls

Course-derived · MIT four-way half-size exercise, positive exact toll. Classify T(n) = 4T(n/2) + 3n, with positive constant bases.

Solution. The critical exponent is log2 4 = 2, while the toll exponent is one. The gap is a full power, satisfying leaf dominance with ε = 1. At depth j, internal contribution is 3n·2j, which grows to order n2 near the bottom. There are n2 leaves with constant positive cost, establishing a matching lower bound. Thus T(n) = Θ(n2). Reducing the internal linear toll to a constant cannot beat that leaf population; changing the branching pattern is necessary for a smaller exponent in this model.

Tutorial 17. Fractional tolls and exact exponents

Course-derived · Stanford's fractional-power concept check. Classify T(n) = 3T(n/81) + 10n1/4 on an ideal admissible grid.

Solution. The critical exponent is log813 = 1/4, because 811/4 = 3. The toll is exactly balanced, so T(n) = Θ(n1/4log n). The regularity ratio is one, not less than one, which is consistent with balanced work rather than root dominance. A quarter-power toll is not a linear toll, and rounding its exponent to a decimal approximation is unnecessary. For a mathematical real-size grid, fractional local weights are legitimate; a literal machine operation count would need an appropriate integer-cost interpretation.

Tutorial 18. A parameter phase transition

Course-derived · Cornell's variable-shrink-factor discussion; changed branching count. Classify T(n) = 9T(n/b) + n2 for fixed b>1.

Solution. Compare p = logb 9 with two. Equality occurs at b = 3. If 1<b<3, the critical exponent exceeds two and leaves dominate, giving Θ(nlogb 9). At three, every internal level contributes order n2, giving Θ(n2 log n). If b>3, the regularity ratio is 9/b2<1, so the answer is Θ(n2). State the threshold and valid parameter domain; a shrink factor of one would not reduce the problem. The answer changes by a logarithm at equality rather than jumping directly between pure powers.

Tutorial 19. A correct order with a failed induction

Course-derived · Cornell's slack technique; changed recursive argument. Prove a linear upper bound for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1, T(1) = 1.

Solution. A bare hypothesis T(k) ≤ Ck yields T(n) ≤ Cn + 1, which does not close for any fixed C. Strengthen the claim to T(k) ≤ Ck − 1. Then the parent is at most 2(Cn/2 − 1) + 1 = Cn − 1. The base requires 1 ≤ C − 1, so choose C = 2. This yields T(n) ≤ 2n − 1, in fact an equality for the exact recurrence. The asymptotic guess was correct; the failed proof lacked a constant amount of slack. This pattern is different from a recurrence whose balanced linear toll truly requires an extra logarithm.

Tutorial 20. A wrong order exposed by constants

Course-derived · CMU's seven-way balanced example; independent proof diagnosis. Why cannot T(n) = 7T(n/7) + n, T(1) = 0, be proved linear by substituting Cn?

Solution. The attempted parent bound becomes 7(Cn/7) + n = (C + 1)n. The coefficient increases at each expansion, so it is not a fixed constant. At depth log7 n, each internal level contributes n, giving the exact result n log7 n on powers of seven. The zero leaves do not contribute here, but the internal levels alone prove the logarithmic factor. This exception to the default positive-base convention is stated explicitly. Induction with n log7 n closes exactly, showing how a failed linear guess can suggest the missing factor.

Tutorial 21. A logarithmic critical toll

Course-derived · MIT's extended balanced case. Classify T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log2 n, with a constant base at one.

Solution. Let n = 2h. The cost at depth j is n(h − j), so internal work is n(h + (h − 1) + … + 1) = nh(h + 1)/2. Add the linear leaf contribution. The total is Θ(n(log n)2). The classical balanced case with toll Θ(n) alone does not cover this toll, but the extended case with log exponent one does. The explicit arithmetic sum proves the added logarithm and prevents treating the toll as a polynomially larger function.

Tutorial 22. A reciprocal-log boundary

Course-derived · Cornell's uncovered recurrence, tightened independently. Solve the order of T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/log2 n, with bases through two and inputs powers of two.

Solution. Normalize at n = 2h by dividing by n. The relation becomes U(h) = U(h − 1) + 1/h, starting at h = 1. Therefore U(h) = U(1) + Hh − 1, giving T(n) = Θ(n log log n). The classical leaf case cannot be used: n/log n is not polynomially below n. Comparing to a larger linear-toll envelope does give O(n log n), but that is not tight. The harmonic depth sum provides the missing precision.

Tutorial 23. Negative logarithmic exponents have a threshold

Original · Complete critical table. Classify T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n2/(log2 n)3/2, with a base range through two.

Solution. The critical exponent is two and the log exponent is negative three halves, below negative one. Reversing the depth index gives normalized total 1 + ∑r = 1hr − 3/2. That sum converges to a finite positive limit, so the total is Θ(n2). The leaves alone already force this order. Blindly adding one to the log exponent would predict n2/√log n, smaller than the compulsory leaf cost. The finite base threshold prevents evaluating the reciprocal logarithm at one.

Tutorial 24. A noninteger logarithmic exponent above the boundary

Original · Integral power sum. Classify T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/√log2 n, with bases through two.

Solution. The normalized depth sum is 1 + ∑ r − 1/2. An integral comparison with 1/√x puts it between positive constant multiples of √h. Hence the answer is Θ(n√log n). This is a critical exponent with log exponent negative one half, which lies above negative one. It is neither a classical leaf case nor the harmonic boundary. Comparing only the sign of the log exponent would miss the distinction between this recurrence and the previous one.

Tutorial 25. Growth alone does not imply regularity

Original · Oscillating toll counterexample. On n = 2h, let T(1) = 1, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + f(n), and let f(n) be n2 at even h and n3 at odd h. Can root dominance be inferred from f(n) ≥ n2?

Solution. For even h ≥ 2, the child exponent index is odd, so the two immediate child tolls already total 2(n/2)3 = n3/4. The parent's toll is only n2, yielding T(n)/f(n) ≥ n/4. The ratio is unbounded along those inputs; T(n) = Θ(f(n)) is false. Regularity would require 2f(n/2)/f(n) bounded by one fixed number below one, while here it equals n/4. A polynomial lower estimate for the toll verifies only one of the root-case hypotheses and cannot replace the other.

Tutorial 26. A theorem can fail while its conclusion remains true

Original · Comparison envelopes. Suppose an equal-size recurrence has nonnegative toll f(n) with n2 ≤ f(n) ≤ 10n2, but the ratio 2f(n/2)/f(n) sometimes exceeds one. Determine the order for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + f(n).

Solution. Use two exact envelope recurrences with tolls n2 and 10n2, and base costs bounding the actual bases. Comparison induction sandwiches the actual cost between them. Each envelope has order n2, as shown by its geometric level sum, so the actual cost has the same order. The displayed regularity condition may fail for the oscillating toll, preventing that direct theorem application. Nevertheless, its bounded monomial envelopes give an independent proof. Failure of a sufficient hypothesis does not imply failure of the conclusion itself.

Tutorial 27. Exact rounding changes lower terms

Course-derived · Princeton's exact split-count theme; actual comparison toll. Compute the balanced merge worst-case comparison counts at n = 5 and n = 8, and give the exact general formula.

Solution. For five, split into two and three. The values at two and three are one and three, so C(5) = 1 + 3 + 4 = 8. For eight, the formula with h = 3 gives C(8) = 8·3 − 8 + 1 = 17. Generally, the balanced tree's leaf depths sum to nh − 2h + n; subtracting one for each of its n − 1 internal nodes gives C(n) = nh − 2h + 1, where h = ⌈log2 n⌉. A reference formula using toll n instead gives a larger answer by n − 1. Exact rounding and the primitive being counted must both match before transferring a formula.

Tutorial 28. A ceiling with an additive offset

Original · Termination and rounding. Analyze T(n) = T(⌈n/2⌉ + 1) + 1 with bases for n ≤ 4.

Solution. For n>4, the child is smaller than the parent. Write the child as at most n/2 + 3/2. Subtract three from the current size: the child's shifted size is at most half the parent's shifted size. Thus after O(log n) calls the input reaches the constant base region. Conversely, each step's argument is at least n/2, so a fixed number fewer than a constant multiple of log n calls cannot reduce a large input to four. With unit local cost and positive bases, the answer is Θ(log n). The additive offset changes a stopping threshold, not the order, and its harmlessness has been proved rather than assumed.

Tutorial 29. Unequal ratios with total mass below one

Course-derived · CMU selection recurrence; independent complete cost bound. Classify an exact positive-toll model T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + n with fixed positive bases.

Solution. Total child size is nine tenths of the parent. Internal linear work at depth j is at most n(9/10)j, so all internal levels total at most 10n. Leaf costs are also O(n) because each stopping leaf has size bounded below by a positive constant and splitting does not increase total mass. The root alone costs n, proving the lower bound. Hence the answer is Θ(n). For an upper inequality with only an O(n) toll, this argument supplies O(n); the actual algorithm's mandatory scan must establish its linear lower bound separately.

Tutorial 30. Rounding the unequal recurrence

Original · Explicit substitution margin. Prove an upper linear bound when T(n) ≤ T(⌈n/5⌉) + T(⌈7n/10⌉) + n above a sufficiently large fixed base threshold.

Solution. The two child sizes sum to at most 0.9n + 2. A naive linear hypothesis then gives at most 0.9Cn + 2C + n, which is bounded by Cn once (0.1C − 1)n ≥ 2C. Choosing C ≥ 20 makes the coefficient at least 0.05C, so the condition holds for n ≥ 40. Choose a constant base threshold of forty, ensuring smaller children, and enlarge C if needed to dominate every positive base ratio T(k)/k for 1 ≤ k ≤ 40. The same C then closes every larger step. This is a complete finite-threshold proof; the ceiling terms have been retained in the inequality.

Tutorial 31. Unequal conserved mass

Course-derived · Cornell's intended unequal-tree example, corrected notation. Classify T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n with fixed positive bases in the ideal model.

Solution. The two fractions sum to one. Akra–Bazzi gives critical exponent one because (1/3)1 + (2/3)1 = 1. The normalized toll integrand is u/u2 = 1/u; its integral grows as log n. Thus T(n) = Θ(n log n). This conclusion also follows by counting conserved mass across full live levels and charging the remaining levels carefully, but a longest-path estimate alone gives only an upper bound. The expression T(n/3) + 2T(n/3) has three equal one-third calls and describes a different tree, even though its asymptotic order happens to agree for a linear toll.

Tutorial 32. A root below one for unequal branches

Course-derived · Princeton Exercise 2.73, independently justified. Classify T(n) = T(n/2) + T(n/4) + n.

Solution. The critical equation is 2 − p + 4 − p = 1. Set z = 2 − p to get z + z2 = 1, whose positive solution is (√5 − 1)/2. Thus p = log2((1 + √5)/2)<1. The linear toll exponent is larger than the critical exponent, and the Akra–Bazzi integral grows as n1 − p; multiplying by np gives Θ(n). The total child mass is three quarters, giving an independent geometric-mass proof. Computing p is not required for that simpler proof, but it verifies the generalized theorem's prediction.

Tutorial 33. A nontrivial critical weighted equation

Course-derived · MIT Akra–Bazzi example, explicit evaluation. Solve the order of T(n) = 2T(n/4) + 3T(n/6) + n log n.

Solution. At exponent one, 2/4 + 3/6 = 1, so uniqueness of the decreasing characteristic expression gives p = 1. The integrand is (u log u)/u2 = (log u)/u. Its integral from a fixed positive cutoff to n is one half of (log n)2 plus a constant. The full answer is therefore Θ(n(log n)2). Choosing one average child size would lose both multiplicities and could produce the wrong critical exponent. The integral's extra one accounts for base work even when the normalized toll integral converges in other examples.

Tutorial 34. Prove an unequal quadratic envelope

Course-derived · Stanford solved substitution concept check. Prove T(n) ≤ 6n2 for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 3T(n/3) + n2, assuming the fixed base interval already satisfies this bound.

Solution. The weighted quadratic child factor is 2/4 + 3/9 = 5/6. Substituting the induction hypothesis gives 2·6(n/2)2 + 3·6(n/3)2 + n2 = 6n2. Thus the bound closes with equality in its envelope. The positive quadratic root toll also gives an Ω(n2) lower bound for the exact recurrence, so its order is quadratic. A guessed upper coefficient two would fail the inequality because 2(5/6) + 1>2. The constant six is an algebraic threshold, not a value chosen from numerical fitting.

Tutorial 35. A nonlinear reduction becomes linear after taking logs

Original · Change of variables. Classify T(n) = 2T(√n) + log2 n on n = 22h with a fixed positive base region.

Solution. Set m = log2 n and S(m) = T(2m). A square-root child has new argument m/2, and the toll is m. Thus S(m) = 2S(m/2) + m, a balanced recurrence with Θ(m log m) growth. Return to the original variable: T(n) = Θ(log n log log n). The admissible grid makes the transformed sequence reach its fixed base exactly. An answer expressed in m is unfinished until the original variable is restored.

Tutorial 36. An exponential toll is outside the integral theorem

Course-derived · Princeton Exercise 2.71 theme; fixed branching. Classify T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 2n on powers of two.

Solution. The root gives T(n) ≥ 2n. For sufficiently large n, a proposed upper bound C2n gives 2C2n/2 + 2n ≤ C2n; choose C ≥ 2 and a fixed threshold where 21 − n/2 ≤ 1/2, then enlarge C for the finite base band. Thus T(n) = Θ(2n). The exponential toll fails multiplicative-interval comparability, so the stated Akra–Bazzi integral formula is not the justification. Direct substitution verifies root dominance under an appropriate condition instead of applying a theorem outside its domain.

Tutorial 37. Work and span have different branching

Original · Parallel model. Two half-size children can execute in parallel, and combining has linear work but logarithmic span. Determine work and span.

Solution. Work sums all executed operations, giving W(n) = 2W(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n). Span follows the slower of the concurrent children and then the combine span: S(n) = S(n/2) + Θ(log n). On n = 2h, its tolls are h,h − 1,…,1, whose arithmetic sum is Θ(h2), so span is Θ((log n)2). This requires a real combine algorithm with logarithmic span and sufficient available parallelism. Using the work recurrence for span would incorrectly count simultaneous children sequentially.

Tutorial 38. Time does not determine live space

Original · Storage liveness. A sequential recursive routine makes two half-size calls. Compare constant-size frames with frames retaining local arrays proportional to their input size.

Solution. With constant frames, only one active root-to-leaf chain needs stack storage at a time, so the recurrence uses a maximum child rather than the sum: M(n) = M(n/2) + Θ(1) = Θ(log n). If every active frame retains a local size-proportional array while recursing, the storage along a halving chain sums n + n/2 + n/4 + …, giving Θ(n). Counting all nodes in the execution tree would count memory from calls that are no longer live. The result also changes if arrays are freed before recursion or shared through an explicit workspace; specify allocation lifetime before writing a storage recurrence.

Tutorial 39. Memoization replaces a tree with a dependency graph

Original · Repeated Fibonacci states. Compare naive Fibonacci calls and a memoized implementation under unit-cost arithmetic.

Solution. The naive call count satisfies N(n) = N(n − 1) + N(n − 2) + 1, with one call at each base. Setting B(n) = N(n) + 1 gives the homogeneous Fibonacci relation, so N(n) = 2Fn + 1 − 1 and its order is exponential in the golden-ratio power. Memoization computes each index once: there are only n + 1 distinct states and a constant number of dependency edges per state, giving linear arithmetic work. Recursive depth can still be linear. This distinction is about the actual execution graph. For bit complexity, additions act on growing Fibonacci integers and need a separate size-sensitive analysis.

Tutorial 40. Expected size is not expected cost

Original · Random-size boundary. A child size is zero or two with equal probability. If its cost is squared size, compare expected cost with the cost at the expected size.

Solution. The expected child size is (0 + 2)/2 = 1. The expected cost is (02 + 22)/2 = 2, whereas cost at the expected size is 12 = 1. Thus replacing E[T(X)] by T(E[X]) loses information about the distribution. An expected algorithm recurrence must condition on the child's actual size, multiply each conditional cost by its probability, and sum. Linearity of expectation applies to sums of random costs without requiring independence, but it does not move expectation through a nonlinear function. This is the precise modeling error behind many apparently plausible average-size recurrences.

Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q130 — A prefix-sum recurrence

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 28 · question 130. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Let c0=1 and cn+1=∑i=0nci for n≥0. Its generating function is C(x)=(1−x)/(1−αx). What is α?

1.
2
2.
3
3.
4
4.
5
Read the complete derivation, base checks and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 1.

Subtract two consecutive prefix equations before introducing a generating function. The first term is c1=c0=1. For n≥1, the two defining equations give

cn+1−cn=∑i=0nci−∑i=0n−1ci=cn.

Thus cn+1=2cn for n≥1, and cn=2n−1 for every n≥1. The qualification is essential: applying c1=2c0 would contradict the original seed. The first six values are 1,1,2,4,8,16.

Treat the generating function as a formal power series, so convergence is unnecessary for coefficient identities. Its constant coefficient is one; the remaining coefficients sum to

C(x)=1+∑n=1∞2n−1xn=1+x1−2x=1−x1−2x.

Comparison with the given denominator gives α=2, option 1. If an analytic interpretation is desired, the geometric-series equality holds for |x|<1/2.

There is an independent coefficient check that diagnoses every wrong option. Expanding the proposed expression for any candidate α gives a coefficient of x equal to α−1. The recurrence requires that coefficient to be c1=1. Options 2, 3 and 4, with α=3,4,5, would instead give 2,3,4. They already fail at the first nonconstant coefficient. Do not solve an altered recurrence with the seed doubled, and do not confuse the denominator growth factor with the exceptional initial term.

Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q1 — Unequal recursive splits

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 1. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Fixed positive constants α,β satisfy α+β=1. For T(n)=T(αn)+T(βn)+n with constant small-input base cost, which listed bound is correct?

1.
O(αβn)
2.
O(nlogn)
3.
O(βnαlogn)
4.
O(αn+βlogn)
Read the complete derivation, base checks and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 2.

Use mass conservation to prove both bounds for the unequal tree. Let B>0 be the fixed stopping size, δ=min(α,β) and q=max(α,β). Because both constants are positive and sum to one, 0<δ≤q<1. First analyze the stated real-size recurrence, which keeps the exact identities visible.

At depth j, every node has size between nδj and nqj. While the smaller bound exceeds B, the entire level remains internal. Its sizes sum to n: each split replaces size s by αs+βs=s. Therefore each of Θ(logn) complete levels contributes exactly n toll, proving Ω(nlogn).

Every branch stops after at most log1/q(n/B)+O(1) levels. On any incomplete level, internal-node sizes total at most n, because terminated subtrees contribute no further internal work. All internal tolls are consequently O(nlogn). Every nonroot leaf has size in (δB,B]; leaf sizes sum to n. There are O(n) leaves, whose bounded base costs add only O(n). This proves the matching upper bound and T(n)∈Θ(nlogn).

Option 2 is the stated valid upper bound. Options 1 and 4 have only linear order for fixed α,β, which is too small. The ratio of option 3 to the derived order is βnα−1→0, so that upper bound also fails. Fixed ratios matter: permitting α to approach zero with the input changes the constants and can invalidate this uniform argument. For an implementation with integer children, declare the rounding and verify progress; the exact real-size identities are not automatically exact integer identities.

Question 3. PhD CE 1405, Q2 — A polylogarithmic toll

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 2. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

What is the order of T(n)=T(2n/3)+log2n, with bounded base cost?

1.
Θ(n)
2.
Θ(log2n)
3.
Θ(log3n)
4.
Θ(nlog2n)
Read the complete derivation, base checks and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 3.

Count a single chain of decreasing logarithms. Choose natural logarithms for the derivation; another fixed base changes only positive constants. Put L=lnn and d=ln(3/2)>0. After j recursive steps, the argument is (2/3)jn, so its toll is (L−jd)2. A fixed stopping threshold gives h=L/d+O(1) nonbase calls. Unrolling yields

T(n)=O(1)+∑j=0h−1(L−jd)2.

There are O(L) summands, each at most L2, giving O(L3). To prove the lower bound, keep the first ⌊L/(2d)⌋ calls. Each has logarithm at least L/2, so these Θ(L) calls contribute Ω(L3). Both bounds establish Θ(log3n), option 3.

The exact subsequence n=(3/2)h, with a base at one, provides a check: the nonrecursive sum is

d2∑r=1hr2=d2h(h+1)(2h+1)6.

The cubic power comes from accumulating squared logarithms along one branch; there are no exponentially many nodes to count.

Option 2 retains just the largest toll and loses a factor of logn. Option 1 asserts a tight linear order, but log3n/n→0. Option 4 is also a false tight order, since (nlog2n)/log3n=n/logn→∞. These two larger expressions would be valid loose upper bounds if they used O; here they use Θ. Fixed bounded integer rounding changes only the final endpoint and constants when the child eventually enters the declared base region.

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 13 · question 58. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Which listed bound describes T(n)=2T(⌊n⌋)+logn with bounded base cost?

1.
O(lognloglogn)
2.

Read the complete derivation, base checks and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 1.

Use the four options actually printed on the enlarged original page. They are O(lognloglogn), O(nlognloglogn), O(nloglogn) and O(loglogn), respectively. The original literal wording admits three true upper bounds. Option 1 is the intended answer under the smallest-listed-upper-bound convention; options 2 and 3 must not be called false upper bounds.

Put m=log2n. Without rounding, the transformed recurrence is S(m)=2S(m/2)+m, whose level toll is 2j(m/2j)=m. There are Θ(logm) nonbase levels and O(m) leaves. Thus S(m)∈Θ(mlogm).

The floor needs an actual bound. For x≥4, x/2≤⌊x⌋≤x. Taking logarithms gives a transformed child between m/2−1 and m/2. Iterating bounds the common size at depth j between m/2j−2 and m/2j. Total toll is at most m and, while 2j≤m/4, at least m−2j+1≥m/2. There are Θ(logm) such early levels. The complete tree stops by O(logm) depth and has O(m) leaves. These independent lower and upper estimates retain the same tight order despite rounding.

Return to the original variable: mlogm=Θ(lognloglogn). Relative to this expression, option 2 has factor n and option 3 has factor n/logn, both unbounded. Option 4 is too small by a factor of logn. A fixed base region must contain the fixed point one and all other terminal inputs; recursing at one would otherwise fail to terminate. The displayed tree uses an exact double-exponential size to illustrate the derivation, and explicitly identifies that illustrative input rather than pretending to animate every integer.

Question 5. MSc CE 1405, Q59 — An unbalanced pivot selection

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 13 · question 59. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

A quicksort variant sorts the first 2n+1 elements by insertion sort and chooses their median as pivot, then proceeds as ordinary quicksort. Which recurrence describes the worst case, suppressing rounding and constant terms?

1.
T(n)=2T(n−1)+n
2.
T(n)=2T(n)+n
3.
T(n)=2T(n−n)+n
4.
T(n)=T(n−n)+T(n)+n
Read the complete derivation, base checks and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 4.

Derive the branch sizes from the pivot guarantee, not from a preferred theorem. For sufficiently large n, the sample size m=2n+1 is at most n after ordinary rounding. Insertion sort of these Θ(n) sampled elements costs O(m2)=O(n), and the ordinary partition scan performs Θ(n) work. The combined toll is therefore Θ(n) even when the sample happened to be already sorted.

Assume distinct keys. The sample median has at least n sampled keys below it and at least that many above it, suppressing the integer corrections. The global pivot rank cannot be closer than roughly n to either endpoint. Nevertheless all unsampled keys can lie on one side, so the guarantee allows a small side of that order and a large side of order n−n.

The faithful integer worst-case model is a maximization over the allowed ranks:

W(n)=maxr∈Rn(W(r)+W(n−1−r)+Θ(n)),

where Rn excludes the forbidden endpoint ranks. The listed extreme-split abstraction suppresses the pivot, rounding and bounded corrections, yielding T(n−n)+T(n)+n, option 4. It describes the worst permitted imbalance, not the split of every input. A proof that the same extreme choices can be realized recursively needs an adversarial-input argument; the recurrence choice alone is not that proof.

Option 1 creates two almost full-size children and violates disjoint partition sizes. Option 2 accounts for only about 2n elements and omits the large partition. Option 3 again counts two large children whose total size exceeds the parent's available keys. With duplicate keys, an equal-key partition policy must be specified; the distinct-rank guarantee cannot be imported unchanged. This is a modeling question, so applying the equal-ratio Master theorem would miss its central point.

Question 6. PhD CS 1404, Q71 — A multiplicative one-step recurrence

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 16 · question 71. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

For T(n)=2nT(n−1) and T(0)=1, which listed order is correct?

1.
Θ(n2n)
2.
Θ(2nlogn)
3.
Θ(2n2)
4.
Θ((2)n2+n)
Read the complete derivation, base checks and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 4.

Expand a product, not a sum. The recurrence multiplies by 2n at the current step. Repeated substitution gives

T(n)=2n2n−1…21T(0)=2∑j=1nj=2n(n+1)/2.

The empty product at n=0 is one, matching the specified seed. An independent logarithmic derivation puts Ln=log2T(n), so Ln=Ln−1+n and L0=0. Summing this additive recurrence gives exactly the same triangular exponent. The first values are 1,2,8,64,1024.

Option 4 is exact, not merely asymptotically equivalent:

2n(n+1)/2=(2)n2+n.

Option 3 fails as a tight class because its ratio to the exact value is 2(n2−n)/2→∞. Although both exponents have quadratic order, a constant factor inside an exponent cannot be discarded when asserting a Θ relation between the exponentials.

Option 1 has base-two logarithm 2nlog2n, which is smaller than n(n+1)/2 by an unbounded asymptotic factor. Its ratio to the exact value tends to zero. Option 2 likewise has logarithm n+log2logn, only roughly linear. Thus neither can provide a matching lower bound for T.

The broad description 2Θ(n2) is valid, but it encompasses many inequivalent tight exponential classes and would not distinguish options 3 and 4. The base seed also matters: replacing it by zero would make every value zero. The logarithmic animation displays the exponent and actual multipliers so its numerical labels stay readable while the mathematical product remains exact.

Question 7. PhD CS 1404, Q28 — Parity far from the given recurrence values

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 28. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Let an=3an−1+5an−2+4, with a16=1403 and a17=2025. How many of a100,a101,…,a113 are even?

1.
4
2.
5
3.
7
4.
10
Read the complete derivation, base checks and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 1.

Project the recurrence onto the two parity states. Let pn be the residue of an modulo two. Both odd multipliers reduce to one, while four reduces to zero. Therefore

pn≡pn−1+pn−2(mod2).

The given values at indices sixteen and seventeen are both odd, so the initial pair is (1,1). Its next state is (1,0), then (0,1), then (1,1) again. The three-state cycle repeats deterministically: the recurrence on pairs maps each current pair to exactly one next pair.

From the anchored indices we obtain p18=0, p19=1, p20=1 and p21=0. Thus the even terms are precisely those indices congruent to zero modulo three along this forward recurrence. We do not need the huge actual values of the sequence.

The closed requested interval contains the multiples 102,105,108,111. Equivalently, their count is

⌊1133⌋−⌊993⌋=37−33=4.

Option 1 is correct. Option 2 would come from including the next multiple, 114, which is outside the interval, or misaligning the initial cycle. Options 3 and 4 do not follow from the actual three-state orbit; the interval has fourteen terms but parity is not evenly alternating.

A bare statement that the cycle has length three is insufficient: its phase must be fixed from the supplied indices. Also, taking parity after numerically generating large integers is unnecessary and obscures the proof. The diagram shows both the initial transition cycle and the actual requested indices, with the skipped middle interval clearly declared. The argument is a finite-state recurrence calculation, not an assumption that all second-order sequences have this period.

Question 8. An exact balanced recurrence

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Independently authored recurrence problem. It is not attributed to an unrelated authentic question.

T(1)=3 and T(n)=2T(n/2)+n for powers of two. What is T(32)?

1.
160
2.
192
3.
256
4.
96
Read the complete derivation, base checks and individual option diagnoses

Correct option: 3.

Keep the base contribution when asking for an exact value. Write n=2h and normalize Vh=T(2h)/2h. The defining recurrence becomes Vh=Vh−1+1, while V0=T(1)=3. Consequently Vh=3+h, and

T(n)=n(3+log2n).

For n=32=25, this is 32(3+5)=256, option 3. The recurrence itself supplies a second exact check: its values at inputs 1,2,4,8,16,32 are 3,8,20,48,112,256.

The tree explains every term. At each of the five internal depths, there are 2j nodes of size 32/2j, so the total toll is 32. Those levels cost 5·32=160. There are 32 leaves and each costs three, adding 96. The total is 160+96=256.

Option 1, 160, drops all leaf work. Option 4, 96, drops all internal work. Option 2, 192, is the answer to a different recurrence with unit leaf cost: its six equal 32-unit contributions would total 192. Exact seed changes can matter even though all these positive fixed seeds preserve the same Θ(nlogn) class.

This derivation uses powers of two, as the question specifies. It is not an exact formula for a rounded implementation at arbitrary sizes. If the input were 33, one would first need the floor/ceiling split and the terminal conditions. The animation accounts for a complete level by node multiplicity rather than drawing dozens of overlapping leaf boxes, and separately includes the base level.
